Three ways to get a more precise treatment effect out of a sample you cannot
grow. All of them work by choosing *which* random split you end up with,
rather than by collecting more units.

<!-- Every figure below is computed in the articles. If the datasets or seeds
     change, re-check these three claims:
       3x and 2%  -> posts/pairwise-matching, "What it is worth on two real
                     datasets" (Project STAR and National Supported Work)
       40% / less powerful
                  -> posts/pairwise-matching, "Analysing a matched
                     experiment" and "A conservative interval is not always a
                     safe one" -->

::: {.keybox}
**Choosing the split well can be worth three times the sample.** Take 400
pupils from Project STAR, pair them on last year's test scores, then flip a
coin inside each pair. That gives the precision of 1,200 pupils split by a
plain coin flip.
:::

::: {.keybox}
**On other data the same method is worth 2%.** Run it on the units of
LaLonde's job-training experiment and it buys almost nothing, because those
covariates barely predict earnings. The method is not what varies here. The
data is, and you can measure which case you are in before you commit.
:::

::: {.keybox}
**Analysed the obvious way, a matched experiment can be worse than no
matching at all.** The gain lives in the pairing, and a standard two-sample
test cannot see it: the confidence interval comes out 40% too wide, and
against small effects it rejects *less* often than if you had never bothered
matching.
:::

Pairwise matching and rerandomization are the two methods. The Mahalanobis
distance is the measure of "alike" that both are built on, and is worth
reading when you want to know why correlated covariates are counted once, or
what makes the distance fail quietly.

All the code is Python, every figure is reproducible from the source, and the
whole thing lives in
[the repository](https://github.com/AlexanderDBolton/BoostSampleSize).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Series status

*Pairwise matching*, *Rerandomization* and *The Mahalanobis distance* are
written. *Stratification* exists as an outline and is not yet published.
:::
